title.$t: PROFESSIONAL BIOGRAPHY

content.$t:
SAMWEL JOHN MUSHI

J.M. Samwel  |  Tanzanian Optometrist

Professional Journey  •  2017–2026

Born 15 April 1997  •  Tanzania

“What started as an idea to serve communities gradually became a professional journey through private practice, community service, consultancy, public education and, ultimately, public service.”


My Professional Journey

My professional journey in Optometry began in 2017. Since then, it has developed through several important stages: professional training, private-sector experience, solo practice, community eye-health initiatives, consultancy, healthcare-worker training, media-based public education and, most recently, a transition into public-sector service.

Looking back, I see these years not simply as a list of jobs or workplaces, but as connected chapters. Each chapter taught me something different and prepared me for the next stage. At the center of the journey has been a continuing interest in eye health, community service and the belief that professional knowledge should be made accessible to the people who need it.

2017  |  Where It All Began

In 2017, I graduated from the School of Optometry at Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Centre (KCMC), Moshi, after completing my field work at CCBRT (Comprehensive Community Based Rehabilitation in Tanzania) in Dar es Salaam. This marked the beginning of my professional life as an Optometrist.

The same year, an idea that would later become an important part of my professional identity was born: Optsam. The name came from “Opt” for Optometrist and “Sam” for Samwel. At that time, however, Optsam was not simply imagined as a commercial business. The idea was to create a platform through which eye-health outreach, awareness and other non-profit-oriented community initiatives could be supported.

I could not register or develop the idea immediately. I was still under provisional practice, financially unstable and did not have the diagnostic instruments and resources needed to run meaningful outreach programmes. I was also surrounded by friends and colleagues who were passionate about NGO and community initiatives. We had many ideas, but the time and resources were not yet supportive. Rather than abandoning the vision, we decided to keep the ideas alive until the opportunity and resources became available.

2017–2019  |  Learning Before Building

The period from 2017 to 2019 became a foundation-building stage. I worked under provisional status and later became fully registered, gaining experience in private clinics, companies and other private-sector environments.

These experiences allowed me to understand Optometry from different professional perspectives. I learned through direct patient care, exposure to different clinical environments, interaction with other professionals and the practical realities of delivering eye-care services.

2018  |  Expanding My Exposure

In 2018, I had the privilege of working with Diamond Optical Ltd., one of the private-sector environments where I explored Optometry and Ophthalmology extensively. The experience contributed significantly to my practical and professional development.

The same year, I also had the opportunity to participate in an ITV Media programme called “Meza Huru.” The approximately one-hour-and-thirty-minute session focused on educating the public about Glaucoma. This was an important moment because it demonstrated that my role as an Optometrist could extend beyond clinical practice into public education.

2019  |  The Beginning of Solo Practice

By 2019, after gaining professional experience and gradually obtaining diagnostic instruments, I was able to take another important step toward independent practice. I established my consultancy/business identity as “Optsam Eye Care and Optical Workshop Store.”

This represented a significant transition. An idea that had started in 2017 was now becoming a practical professional platform through which I could provide Optometry services and work with different organizations and communities.

2019–2021  |  From Solo Practice to Community Service

Between 2019 and 2021, my professional activities expanded beyond individual clinical practice. I worked with different organizations, schools, churches, community groups, NGOs and polyclinics.

Among the experiences were activities involving TAG Ukonga Church in 2020, the Group of Retired Prison Officers in Ukonga in 2020, Rotary International events in 2020, Tanzanites Lions Club in Dar es Salaam in 2021, Aga Khan Health Services in Tanzania through Aga Khan Polyclinic Tabata in 2021, and Sokeny Polyclinic Mabibo in 2021, among others.

These experiences brought me closer to the community-service spirit that had been part of the original Optsam idea. They also helped me appreciate that eye health can be promoted in many settings, not only inside a clinic.

2021  |  Sharing Knowledge With Healthcare Workers

In 2021, I had another opportunity to contribute beyond direct patient care by facilitating training with Tindwa Medical and Health Services in Tanzania. The training involved healthcare workers, including Doctors and Nurses, and focused on the use of the Snellen Visual Acuity Chart.

This experience strengthened another aspect of my professional identity: sharing practical eye-health knowledge with other healthcare workers so that basic vision assessment can be better understood and applied.

2021–2024  |  A Major Consultancy Chapter

From 2021 to 2024, I had the privilege of serving under a consultancy agreement with Aga Khan Health Services in Tanzania to provide outsourced Optometry services at Aga Khan Polyclinic, Tabata, Dar es Salaam.

This became an important and sustained chapter of my private-sector career. It provided an opportunity to work within an established healthcare environment while continuing to develop professionally through consultancy practice. It also represented a level of institutional trust and responsibility that I value as part of my career development.

2022  |  World Sight Day and School Eye Health

In 2022, I used World Sight Day as another opportunity to contribute to community eye health. I served students at Migombani Secondary School, a government school in Dar es Salaam.

This experience reflected a continuing theme throughout my career: bringing eye-health awareness and services closer to communities, especially through settings such as schools where early awareness can make a meaningful difference.

2025–2026  |  Eye Health Education Through Documentary Media

During 2025 and 2026, my involvement in public education continued through TBC Media in a programme called “Aridhio.” I had the privilege of participating in documentary sessions covering different topics related to health and society.

The documentary topics included the way mobile-phone use can affect social interaction and aspects of eye health, the importance of regular eye check-ups, and Glaucoma. These experiences strengthened my belief that professional knowledge should not remain inside the consulting room. People need understandable information about their health before they become patients.

Late 2025–2026  |  A New Direction: Public Service

Toward the end of 2025, I began deliberately exploring another dimension of my profession: public-sector Optometry. I volunteered for a period at Kigamboni Health Center in Dar es Salaam, using the opportunity to gain an understanding of the public healthcare environment.

I later received an opportunity to serve at Mchemo District Hospital in Mtwara, marking a major transition in my professional journey. For me, this is not simply a change of workplace. It is an opportunity to explore Optometry from another perspective and to understand how my experience can contribute within the public health system.

2017–2026  |  Looking Back With Purpose

When I look back at the period from 2017 to 2026, I do not see only different workplaces or professional titles. I see a gradual process of growth, experimentation, service and learning.

I began as a young Optometrist with an idea. I worked under provisional practice, learned from the private sector, explored Optometry and Ophthalmology, developed solo practice, worked with communities, provided consultancy services, trained healthcare workers, participated in television and documentary education, and eventually entered public-sector service.

The name Optsam, which began in 2017 as an idea to help communities, has remained connected to the deeper purpose of my professional journey. Even as my career environment has changed, the principle of using Optometry to contribute to eye health and public awareness has remained.

The Next Chapter

Today, I am proud of what I have accomplished since 2017. At the same time, I recognize that professional growth does not have a final destination.

“The private sector taught me independence.
Community work taught me service.
Consultancy taught me responsibility.
Media taught me the power of education.
And public service is now giving me a new perspective.”

My next chapter is therefore not about forgetting where I came from. It is about taking everything I have learned and asking how I can use my experience, knowledge and profession to create greater impact.

SAMWEL JOHN MUSHI (J.M. SAMWEL)
Tanzanian Optometrist
2017–2026 — A Journey of Practice, Service, Learning and Purpose.

title.$t: OFFICIAL STATEMENT ASK OPTSAM — TANZANIAN INITIATIVE FOR EYE-HEALTH EDUCATION

content.$t:
Optsam was never just a name. It has always been a vision and a journey.

I am Samwel John Mushi, born 15th April 1997 professionally known as J.M. Samwel, Optometrist.

I would like to take this opportunity to formally clarify the meaning, history and current direction of Optsam, particularly the development of Ask Optsam, as I continue my professional journey in eye health.

The Beginning — 2017

The Optsam journey began in 2017, rooted in my profession as an Optometrist.

The name OPT was derived from Optometrist, while SAM was derived from Samwel — reflecting my name and professional identity as Samwel / J.M. Samwel / Samwel John Mushi.

From its beginning, Optsam was founded around a vision of contributing to the community through eye-health education, awareness and activities intended to address avoidable blindness and visual impairment.

The founding concept and objectives of Optsam were primarily non-profit and community-oriented.

Understanding “Optsam Eye Care and Optical Workshop Store”

At one stage of this journey, Optsam Eye Care and Optical Workshop Store became the business identity through which I conducted private-sector professional activities.

It is important to clarify that this business identity represented the commercial side of my professional practice, while the broader Optsam vision extended beyond commercial activities.

During my private practice, the business component helped provide resources that supported various ideas, programmes and community-oriented activities associated with the vision I had developed.

There were also situations in which institutional clients required consultation and professional services to be invoiced under a registered business name. This contributed to the adoption and use of Optsam Eye Care and Optical Workshop Store as a trading identity.

However, the existence of that business identity should not be interpreted as meaning that the original vision of Optsam was established solely for profit.

The people who joined me during different stages of that journey were largely friends, colleagues and supporters who willingly contributed their time, knowledge and effort toward ideas they believed in.

A Journey of Ideas

Over the years, Optsam became more than a name or a single activity. It became a source of ideas.

One of those ideas eventually became Ask Optsam.

Ask Optsam represents my continued exploration of how responsible use of the internet can expand access to reliable eye-health information, education and awareness.

The initiative is intended to provide information about eye health in Kiswahili and English, with content relevant to the needs and realities of Tanzania, and with the long-term vision of reaching communities across East Africa.

Its purpose is educational and awareness-oriented: to help people understand eye health, visual impairment, avoidable blindness, prevention, appropriate eye-care seeking and the importance of professional eye-care services.

My Transition to Public Service

This year marks another important chapter in my professional journey.

After years of practising Optometry in the private sector — including spending a significant part of my professional practice as a solo practitioner — I have now officially transitioned into public service.

I consider this an important opportunity to serve, learn and understand the delivery of primary eye care from another perspective.

My experience in the private sector has shaped my understanding of patients, communities, professional practice and the challenges surrounding access to eye care. I believe that this experience can contribute positively to my public-service journey while maintaining the highest standards of professional ethics, integrity and responsibility.

Separation of Roles and Commitment to Integrity

Because I now serve in the public sector, I also recognise the importance of transparency and avoiding any actual or perceived conflict of interest.

For that reason, it is important to make the position of Ask Optsam clear.

Ask Optsam is a personal, non-commercial, educational and eye-health awareness initiative. It is not a government programme, does not represent the Government of Tanzania, and should not be interpreted as speaking on behalf of my employer or any government institution.

The initiative is also not intended to replace eye-care professionals, replace clinical services, solicit patients, compete with public health services, or interfere with my official responsibilities as a public servant.

My government duties and professional responsibilities remain separate from the activities and identity of Ask Optsam.

Any information shared through Ask Optsam is intended primarily for general education and awareness. Where individual clinical assessment, diagnosis, treatment or other professional intervention is required, members of the public should seek care from qualified and appropriate eye-health professionals or health facilities.

I am committed to ensuring that my personal initiative does not compromise my responsibilities, professional ethics, impartiality or obligations as a public servant.

Why Continue Optsam?

Some may ask why I continue with Optsam after moving from private-sector practice into public service.

The answer is simple:

I do not want to abandon a vision that has been part of my journey for nearly nine years simply because my professional circumstances have changed.

Instead, I believe the vision can evolve into a form that is more appropriate to my current professional position.

The journey that once included a business-oriented identity can now increasingly focus on the social-impact and educational side of the original vision.

That is where Ask Optsam comes in.

It is an attempt to use knowledge, technology and responsible digital communication to contribute to the fight against avoidable blindness and visual impairment through education and awareness.

What Optsam Means Today

Optsam is not simply a business name.

Optsam is a vision.

Optsam is a journey.

Optsam is a collection of ideas that continue to evolve.

And Ask Optsam is one chapter of that journey — a chapter focused on eye-health education, public awareness and responsible sharing of knowledge.

My transition into public service does not end that journey.

It gives it a new responsibility.

I intend to continue developing Ask Optsam in a way that respects professional boundaries, public-service responsibilities, ethical standards and the trust of the community.

My hope is that this platform can contribute, even in a small way, to a more informed society — one that understands the importance of eye health, recognises the risks of avoidable blindness and visual impairment, and knows when and where to seek appropriate professional care.

The name may evolve.
The structure may change.
The chapter may be different.
But the vision remains.

Ask Optsam

Tanzanian Initiative for Eye-Health Education

Reliable Eye-Health Information • Education • Awareness

J.M. Samwel, Optometrist
Optsam

content.$t:
Kuona ni kuamini ; Seeing is believing 

(Documentary Script)


All rights reserved 2019


Episode1

Written by J.M.Samwel, Optometrist 

T/A Optsam

2019


Mathayo 6:22

“Jicho ni taa ya mwili. Kama basi jicho lako ni zima, mwili wako wote utakuwa katika mwanga.”


Oxford’s language Dictionary 

See

To perceive with the eyes; discern visually.

Believe 

To accept that (something) is true, even if you don’t have proof 


Optsam : Seeing is believing 


Kuona ni kutambua na kukubali kuwa ni kweli sasa..


Idadi ya watu vipofu duniani inaongezeka kwa kasi zaidi kuliko idadi ya watu duniani inavyoongezeka.


Angalau watu bilioni 2.2 wana matatizo ya uoni, na kati yao, angalau watu bilioni 1 wana matatizo ya kuona ambayo yanaweza kuzuilika au bado 


Samwel John, born 15th april 1997,Tanzanian Optometrist T/A Optsam eye care and optical workshop store ©️2019 (Check Optsam®️ Bio.)


Watu wengi wanachagua bila hiari/ bila kufahamu kutoshughulika na afya za macho yao kutokana  na kuhisi kuona bado wanaweza kuendelea na shughuli zao wanazofanya kila siku bila vikwazo.


Jicho ni kiungo chenye muundo wa ajabu na mgumu kujifunza katika mwili wa binadamu. 


Macho mawili hutoa karibu nusu ya hisia zote za mwili mzima kuelekea kwenye ubongo kwa ajili ya  kuona.


Hatuoni kwa macho tunaona kwa ubongo

Utambuzi hufanyika katika ubongo hivyo, Jicho ni zana hutumika kwa ajili ya kuona kupitia kichochezi ambacho ni Mwanga


Mwanga ukifika kwenye “pazia la kuona” (Retina) hubadilishwa na kuwa mfumo wa taarifa za fahamu na “seli maalum” kupitia mshipa wa fahamu (Neva ya Optika) na kupelekwa kwenye ubongo kwa ajili ya utambuzi.


Jicho ni kiungo cha nje na hivyo kinakabiliwa sana na mazingira. Kwa hiyo, usafi duni pamoja na lishe,hali ya hewa, wadudu wanaosambaza magonjwa,kuongezeka kwa idadi ya watu,kuzeeka pamoja na mitindo ya maisha, na vingine huchangia kuathiri kwa kiasi kikubwa idadi na aina ya magonjwa ya macho katika jamii.


Nimekuwa nikifanya kazi ya optometria tangu mwaka 2017 kama huduma katika ngazi ya awari/msingi ya utunzaji wa macho ambayo ni uchunguzi wa uoni, utoaji wa miwani tiba, kutambua na kusimamia magonjwa ya macho au kutoa rufaa kwa wataalamu wengine.


“Kuona ni kuamini” ilibuniwa ili kuleta mwanga na sauti itakayowawezesha na kushirikisha watu katika jamii zote zaidi kuhusu elimu ya afya ya macho kama zana kwa ajili ya kuona kupitia programu endelevu kama ilivyopendekezwa na @who kwenye ripoti yake ya World Vision ya mwaka 2020©️. 

Programu hizi zitawashirikisha watu binafsi na familia katika jamii zote kwa kuamini katika kuzuia, kufanya maamuzi na kuhusika kujisimamia kuhusu uwezo wa macho yao kuona.


Watu wakipata elimu kuhusu macho yao , itawaaminisha wao ni wa kwanza kugundua na kuchukulia hatua kila wanapohisi dalili kabla ya ugonjwa kutokea 


Ikiwa macho yetu hayapokei mwanga kwa muda mrefu, yanaweza kuzorota na kusababisha hatari kubwa ya upofu au uoni hafifu. Hali hii inaweza kuchukuliwa kama ulemavu, 


Mtu anaweza kuwa mlemavu wa kuona bila kufahamu na bado akawa na uwezo wa kutembea bila kikwazo/msaada ( Uoni Hafifu ) i.e Albino. 



Episode 2


Overview

Kupitia picha za kuvutia na mahojiano ya wataalamu, Makala hii itatoa uchunguzi wenye maarifa na fupi juu ya jinsi ubongo wetu unavyochakata taarifa za kuona, macho kama zana ya kuona, na hatari na changamoto zinazohusiana na uoni kwa ujumla Duniani.


Katika Makala hii, tutaelezea dhana ya jinsi tunavyoona kwa ubongo wetu badala ya macho yetu. Macho yetu hutumika kama zana ya kuona, lakini yanahitaji vichocheo kutoka nje, ambacho haswa Mwanga, ili kufanya kazi kwa ufanisi. Kama vile gari linahitaji mafuta ili kuendeshwa na mtu, macho yetu yanahitaji mwanga kama chanzo cha nishati ili kutambua vitu katika shughuli zetu za kila siku.


Ulemavu ni hali yoyote ya mwili au akili (upungufu) ambayo inafanya iwe vigumu kwa mtu mwenye hali hiyo kushindwa kufanya shughuli fulani (ukomo wa shughuli) na kuwasiliana na ulimwengu unaonzunguka (vikwazo vya ushirikiano).


Mtu anaweza kuwa mlemavu wa kuona bila kufahamu na bado akawa na uwezo wa kutembea bila kikwazo/msaada ( Uoni Hafifu ) i.e Albino. 


Pua yako huwa unaingalia lakini ubongo wako hauoni kupitia mchakato unaoitwa kitaalamu “Unconscious selectively” uchaguzi bila hiari/ bila kufahamu .


Huoni pua yako kwa sababu ubongo wako hauishughulikii. Ingawa pua yako iko muda wote katika uwanja wako wa kuona, ubongo wako unaiacha kwa sababu sio taarifa unayohitaji kufanyia  katika shughuli za kila siku.


Hatuoni kwa sababu hatushughuliki na Taa inayomulika mwilini”(jicho) na badala yake ubongo unashindwa kupata vizuri taarifa muhimu huihitaji kufanyia kazi katika shughuli zetu za kila siku kwa ajili ya kuona ambayo ni “Mwanga” 


Lesson 


Upofu

Upofu unaweza kutokea ghafla au taratibu huku ikitegemeana na kisababishi.


Kulingana na WHO,Upofu ni uwezo wa kuona chini ya 3/60 kwa jicho bora pamoja na miwani inayofaa zaidi, au upotezaji wa upeo wa kuona chini ya 10 katika uwanja wa kuona. (Upotevu huu wa upeo wa macho unazuia mtu kutembea au kujiongoza kwa uhuru).


Uoni Hafifu

Pia kuna kundi jingine la watu wenye "uoni hafifu" ni uwezo wa kuona chini ya au 6/18 lakini bora kuliko 3/60 kwa jicho bora pamoja na miwani inayofaa zaidi. (Mtu huyu anakuwa na  ulemavu wa kuona lakini anaweza kuzunguka kwa uhuru kabisa).


Mzigo huu haukubebwa sawasawa. Unawalemea zaidi jamii zenye kipato cha chini na cha kati, pamoja na watu wazee, na jamii za vijijini.


Jamii maskini au jamii zinazoendelea, huwa na huduma duni za matibabu na hivyo magonjwa mara nyingi huonekana katika hali mbaya au husahaulika kushughulikiwa.



Watu wanaohitaji huduma ya macho lazima waweze kupata huduma bora, zinazopatikana na kufikika katika maeneo yote ya jamii pasi na kupitia ugumu kifedha.



Malengo yake yanazingatia magonjwa yanayosababisha upofu unaozuilika na kutibika.

i. Kutekeleza IPEC kwa kutoa huduma bora za afya ya macho ambazo zinapatikana na kufikika katika maeneo yote ya jamii.

ii. Kuwezesha jamii za ndani kupokea huduma bora za afya ya macho bila kuteseka kifedha.

iii. Kuwawezesha na kuwashirikisha watu katika jamii kwa kutekeleza programu endelevu za afya ya macho.

iv. Kutoa huduma za afya ya macho zilizoandaliwa vizuri kupitia usimamizi wa kesi, huduma kitimu na mfumo mzuri wa rufaa.


How Optsam operates;

Visiting care

Visiting Doctor/Optometrist that provides a mobile eye care by screening and assessing people in all community settings and give them medical/optical care, those needing more intensive management are then referred to other specialists (Tertiary health care).


Jinsi Optsam inavyofanya kazi;

Huduma ya kutembelea

Kuna Daktari/Mganga anayetoa huduma ya afya ya macho kwa kutembelea.

Huchunguza na kutathmini watu katika jamii na kuwapa huduma za matibabu au ushauri, wale wanaohitaji huduma za uangalizi zaidi hupelekwa kwa wataalamu wengine (huduma ya afya ya ngazi ya juu).


Eye Health Literate care and Training 

“Seeing is believing “  was invented to bring the light and sound that will empower and engage people in all communities about eye health education through sustainable programs as @who recommended on its previous World Vision report 2020©️

These programs engage individuals and families “believing” in prevention, decision making and self-management concern their eyes ability to “see(ing)”.


Skilled based Training within Optometry premises i.e Media Interviews, Visual Acuity Concept. , Presentations, Podcasts , Documentaries etc.





Optsam store

This is an Optical workshop store deals with health and beauty , It provides the selling products and services including therapeutic lenses, cosmetic lenses, brandy frames, spectacles, contact lens fitting, optical accessories etc.


As we reflect on the powerful words of Surah An-Nur Ayat 35 from the Quran, we are reminded that.


“Allah ni Nuru ya mbingu na dunia. Nuru yake ni kama tundu ambayo kuna taa, taa iko katika kioo, kioo ni kama nyota inayong'aa, iliyoung'aa kutokana na mafuta ya mzeituni mwenye baraka, wala haiko upande wa mashariki wala magharibi, ambayo mafuta yake yanaweza kuwaka hata bila kuguswa na moto. Nuru juu ya nuru! Allah anamwongoza yeyote anayemtaka kwenye nuru yake. Na Allah anaweka mfano kwa ajili ya binadamu. Kwani Allah anajua kila kitu kwa ukamilifu.”


With this profound message, we find hope in the increasing awareness of the challenges of treatable and preventable blindness in our world. Governments have formed committees to address the issue on a local level, while funds from organizations like the World Bank support cataract surgeries in countries like India. Moreover, there is a growing recognition of the importance of training and supporting paramedical staff, such as ophthalmic medical assistants, to initiate eye programs.


However, despite these efforts, the number of avoidably blind individuals continues to rise at a faster rate than the world population. It is crucial that we acknowledge this alarming trend and take decisive action to combat it.


Utabiri unaonyesha kuwa mahitaji ya huduma ya macho duniani yataongezeka katika miaka ijayo kutokana na ukuaji wa idadi ya watu, kuzeeka, na mabadiliko katika mtindo wa maisha.


In the words of J.M. Samwel, a dedicated optometrist, "Seeing is believing." Let us strive together to ensure that everyone has the opportunity to see the world and experience its wonders. Only then can we truly make a difference and bring light to the lives of those who need it most.

title.$t: Optsam IPEC program , Integrated People-centered Eye Care at Ukonga , Dar es salaam

content.$t:
Everyone, if they live long enough, will experience at least one eye condition in their lifetime that will require appropriate care.


 Globally, at least 2.2 billion people have a vision impairment or blindness, of whom at least 1 billion have a vision impairment that could have been prevented or has yet to be addressed. Tens of millions have a severe vision impairment and could benefit from rehabilitation which they are not currently receiving. The burden of eye conditions and vision impairment is not borne equally: it is often far greater in low- and middle-income countries, among older people and in women, and in rural and disadvantaged communities.

 

📸 by @suncheafrica , Reference  @who World vision report , Optometrist  J.M.Samwel on the left side with client who attended for eye screening session at Ukonga , Dar es salaam.
